newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine police ready to clear job protests.
newsitem.headline: Argentine police ready to clear job protests.

text.p: Argentine police were told on Thursday to clear roadblocks set up to protest unemployment in the poor province of Jujuy, but held back while unions and church officials negotiated with the local government.

The number of roadblocks in Jujuy more than doubled to 21 with between 30 and 100 people manning each barricade, police said. In Jujuy province, unemployment in some towns is as high as 37 percent versus the national level of 17.3 percent.
The roadblock protests, which began weeks ago in the deep south of Patagonia, have also spread to the central province of Cordoba, where three roads were being blocked.
The Peronist government's termed the protests "criminal" and Federal Judge Horacio Paz ordered the police to go in.

But Jujuy Bishop Marcelo Palentini, mindful of riots in the province last week when more than 100 people were hurt after police tried to clear a roadblock in a shanty town, asked the judge to delay the order while negotiations went on.

"The judge has ordered us to clear the roads, but first we have to warn the protesters, and if they don't move the judge will decide what steps to take," said a spokesman for the paramilitary border police involved in last week's rioting.
One Jujuy provincial police officer told Reuters the situation on the roads was "at an impasse while talks between the bishop, the government and the picketers go on."

"The police are in their barracks and don't want to have to act, because many people on the roadblocks are family," said the officer. "It's a humanitarian situation, people don't have enough to eat and want the province to act."
The CTA labour federation said it was talking with local government and business leaders to seek an answer to the job problem. It warned against any heavy-handed police action.
"At the first sign of repression the people will turn on them. It's characteristic of the people of Jujuy that when you touch one of them, the rest will fight," said a CTA official.
So far, Argentina's Peronist government has offered the province 1,500 temporary jobs -- but the protesters want 5,000 jobs for people laid off from sugar and steel works.
